1970:
Bombardment means the act of hitting something continuously, heavily, and repeatedly — whether with physical weapons, particles of matter, or even non-physical things like words, questions, or messages.

Think of it this way: if something happens to you once, that's just an event. But if it keeps coming at you — again and again, powerfully and relentlessly — that is a bombardment.

1. Military Bombardment (the original and most common meaning)

This is the sustained, heavy attack on a place — a city, a fort, a military position — using weapons like bombs, artillery shells, missiles, or heavy gunfire, usually over a period of time.

The key features that make something a "bombardment" in the military sense:

  • It is continuous or repeated, not a single strike
  • It involves large-scale, heavy firepower
  • It is directed at a specific target or area
  • It often aims to destroy, weaken, or force surrender

Examples:

  • "The bombardment of the coastal city lasted for three days, leaving most of its buildings in ruins."
  • "Citizens hid in underground shelters during the aerial bombardment."
  • "The naval bombardment from warships offshore destroyed the enemy's defences before troops landed."

Notice the word suggests something overwhelming — not a single bullet, but a relentless storm of destruction.

2. Scientific Bombardment (used in physics and chemistry)

In science, bombardment refers to directing a stream of fast-moving particles — like neutrons, protons, or electrons — at a target substance or atomic nucleus.

Scientists do this to study atomic structure, trigger nuclear reactions, or create new elements and isotopes.

Examples:

  • "The bombardment of uranium atoms with neutrons can trigger a chain reaction."
  • "Through particle bombardment, scientists were able to create a new radioactive isotope in the laboratory."

The logic is the same as the military meaning — something is being repeatedly struck by things coming at it — just at an atomic scale.

3. Figurative Bombardment (used in everyday speech and writing)

This is the most flexible use of the word. Here, "bombardment" describes the experience of being overwhelmed by a large, continuous flood of non-physical things — like information, questions, requests, criticism, noise, or stimulation.

You use it whenever something comes at a person in great quantity, without pause, and often in an overwhelming way.

Examples:

  • "The celebrity faced a bombardment of questions from reporters the moment she stepped outside."
  • "After the product launched, the company's inbox received a bombardment of customer complaints."
  • "The student felt mentally exhausted after a bombardment of new information during the lecture."
  • "Modern social media exposes users to a constant bombardment of advertisements."

In everyday language, this is probably the sense you will encounter most often.

No matter the context — military, scientific, or figurative — bombardment always carries the same underlying feeling:

  • Something is coming in large amounts
  • It is relentless and repeated, not a single instance
  • It feels heavy, overwhelming, or hard to escape
  • There is a clear target being hit

This shared feeling is what gives the word its power. Calling something a "bombardment" — even metaphorically — instantly tells your reader or listener that it was not mild or occasional. It was intense, sustained, and hard to withstand.
How the Word Behaves in a Sentence

"Bombardment" is a countable and uncountable noun, meaning you can use it both ways:

  • Uncountable (referring to the general act): "The city suffered weeks of bombardment."
  • Countable (referring to a specific instance): "The bombardment of 1944 is well-documented in history." / "There were multiple bombardments throughout the siege."

It is commonly paired with:

  • Verbs: face, endure, survive, launch, begin, cease, withstand
  • Adjectives: heavy, intense, constant, continuous, aerial, nuclear, relentless, sustained
Strength and Tone of the Word

"Bombardment" is a strong, serious word. It carries a tone of intensity and overwhelm. Even in its figurative use, it is not a neutral word — it signals that the experience was a lot, and likely unpleasant or hard to handle.

Compare these two sentences:

  • "She received many emails." — neutral, calm
  • "She received a bombardment of emails." — intense, overwhelming

The second sentence makes you feel how overwhelming the situation was. That is the specific power this word adds to your language.

ContextWhat it means

To put it simply: a bombardment is the relentless, heavy, repeated striking of something — whether a place is being bombed in war, an atom is being struck by particles in a lab, or a person is being overwhelmed by a flood of questions, messages, or information. The word always signals something intense, sustained, and hard to escape.
1971:
Bombast is language — spoken or written — that sounds grand, powerful, and impressive, but is actually hollow and empty underneath. It is big words, dramatic statements, and inflated claims that carry very little real meaning or truth. It is the verbal equivalent of a beautifully wrapped gift box that turns out to be completely empty inside.

Think of it this way: when someone uses bombast, they are essentially trying to perform importance rather than communicate anything of real value. The words are showy, the tone is solemn and weighty, but if you slow down and ask "wait — what did they actually just say?", the honest answer is: not much.

Bombast has three reliable hallmarks that almost always appear together:

1. Inflated language. The words chosen are far bigger and more complicated than the idea actually needs. Instead of saying "we will do our best," a bombastic speaker might say "we shall pursue, with the full might of our collective resolve, the relentless and unyielding pursuit of excellence in all its manifestations." It means the same thing — or perhaps even less — but it sounds weightier.

2. A gap between sound and substance. This is the defining quality. Bombast is not just fancy language — fancy language used accurately and usefully is fine. Bombast is fancy language that, upon inspection, reveals there is not much behind it. The style massively outweighs the content.

3. The intent to impress. Bombast is not usually accidental. The person using it wants you to be dazzled by how they sound, often because they do not have a strong enough idea to stand on its own. The dazzle is meant to distract you.
A Concrete Example to Make It Click

Imagine a manager addressing their team before a difficult project. Here are two versions of what they might say:

Version A (plain and honest):
"This project will be tough. We have six weeks, the deadline is firm, and we'll need to work hard. I believe we can do it if we stay focused and communicate well."

Version B (bombast):
"We stand at the precipice of a truly historic undertaking — a moment that will define the very soul and character of this team for generations to come. The forces of challenge may be formidable, but the unbreakable spirit of human determination shall blaze a triumphant trail through the darkness of uncertainty, lighting the way toward a glorious and magnificent victory!"

Version B sounds dramatically more exciting. But notice: it tells you absolutely nothing useful. It gives no timeline, no plan, no specific encouragement — just soaring, theatrical language designed to make the speaker sound inspiring and important. That is bombast. And after the applause fades, the team is no better informed than before.

Bombast shows up most commonly in:

  • Politics. Campaign speeches are famously prone to bombast. Phrases like "we will restore the sacred covenant of liberty and forge an unbreakable destiny for the people of this great nation" sound momentous, but they commit to nothing and explain nothing. Voters often walk away feeling stirred but uninformed.
  • Corporate and business language. Phrases like "we are disrupting the paradigm by leveraging synergistic ecosystems to deliver transformative value propositions" are textbook bombast — dense with jargon that sounds sophisticated, but communicates almost nothing to an ordinary person (and sometimes not even to insiders).
  • Self-promotion. Someone who describes a mediocre skill as "a masterful and unparalleled expertise that has reshaped the landscape of the industry" is leaning heavily on bombast to compensate for a lack of actual achievement.
  • Writing. Essays, articles, or speeches that are padded with elaborate vocabulary and theatrical sentences, but lack clear arguments or real information, are guilty of bombast on the page.
How to Spot Bombast in the Wild

Here is a simple test you can apply: after reading or hearing something, ask yourself:

"If I removed all the dramatic, flowery language and just kept the actual facts and ideas — what is left?"

If the answer is a lot, the language was legitimate. If the answer is very little, or nothing, you were just served bombast.

Another clue: bombast often makes you feel moved or impressed in the moment, but leaves you strangely unable to summarize what was actually said. That vagueness after the curtain comes down is a telltale sign.
How It Is Used in Sentences

• "The senator's speech was pure bombast — thirty minutes of soaring phrases, but not a single concrete policy proposal."
  • "I was initially impressed by his pitch, but after re-reading it, I realized it was mostly bombast — nothing but grand promises with no substance."
  • "Cut through the bombast and tell me, in plain language, what your plan actually is."
  • "Her critics accused her of relying on bombast to hide the fact that she had no real answers."

The adjective form is bombastic, and it means "characterized by bombast." You would use it to describe a person, a speech, a piece of writing, or a style that relies on inflated, hollow language.

  • "He was a bombastic speaker — entertaining to watch, but easy to see through."
  • "The essay was well-researched but written in a painfully bombastic style."

The adverb form is bombastically — meaning in a bombastic manner.

One last helpful thing to hold onto: bombast tends to produce a very specific feeling in a perceptive reader or listener — a kind of vague suspicion. Something inside you senses that the person is working very hard to sound impressive, and that effort itself becomes a red flag. Genuine ideas, clearly expressed, rarely need theatrical inflation. When language is turned up to maximum volume for no apparent reason, it is often because the idea underneath cannot carry its own weight.

Knowing the word bombast gives you the vocabulary to name that feeling precisely — and to call it out when you see it.
1972:
Bombastic describes language — speech or writing — that sounds grand, powerful, and deeply impressive on the surface, but is actually hollow and empty underneath. Think of it like a giant, colorful balloon: it looks enormous and eye-catching, but there's nothing inside except air.

When a person speaks or writes in a bombastic way, they use big, dramatic words, exaggerated phrases, and loud declarations — not to communicate something meaningful, but to sound more important, intelligent, or powerful than they really are. The result is all style and no substance. The listener is hit with a wave of impressive-sounding noise but walks away having learned very little.

This is crucial: bombastic is never a compliment. If someone calls your writing or speech "bombastic," they are criticizing it. They're saying it's trying too hard to impress — and the effort is transparent, even a little embarrassing.
Real examples to make it click

The politician. Imagine a leader giving a speech: "We shall rise! We shall conquer! The great destiny of our noble nation demands nothing less than total and glorious victory!" — but they never actually explain what their plan is. There's passion and theatre, but no real information. That's bombastic.

The salesperson. Someone describes a basic kitchen blender as "a revolutionary, groundbreaking, life-transforming instrument of culinary mastery." Bombastic.

The student. Someone writes "The profoundly magnificent complexity of this multidimensional philosophical conundrum necessitates the deepest contemplative engagement" when they simply mean "This is a hard question." Bombastic.

In all three cases, the language is dramatically out of proportion to what is actually being said.
The important distinction: bombastic vs. just "using big words"

Using complex or sophisticated vocabulary is not automatically bombastic. A doctor using precise medical terms is not being bombastic — they're being accurate. A lawyer writing in formal legal language is not bombastic — the language serves a clear purpose.

Bombastic language specifically fails on three grounds. First, the impressive words are chosen to dazzle, not to communicate. Second, the meaning could have been expressed far more simply and clearly. Third, the grandness of the language is wildly out of proportion to the importance of what is actually being said.
How it differs from similar words

Verbose means using too many words, but those words might still be plain and honest. Bombastic specifically means the words are inflated and showy.

Eloquent is almost the opposite of bombastic. An eloquent speaker is also impressive and even moving, but their language is clear and genuine, and it carries real meaning. Eloquence earns its impressiveness. Bombastic language fakes it.

Pretentious is close, but broader. It can describe a person's general attitude or choices — someone who only reads obscure books to seem intellectual is pretentious. Bombastic is specifically about language being puffed up and hollow.

Grandiose overlaps with bombastic, but grandiose focuses more on an attitude of self-importance and exaggerated greatness, while bombastic is specifically about the language being inflated and empty.
A mental picture to remember it forever

Imagine a person at a podium — wearing a dramatic cape, arms raised wide, voice booming across a hushed auditorium. Everyone leans in, expecting profound wisdom. The speech builds and builds... and it turns out the person has been saying, with thunderous emotion and elaborate flourish:

"I believe that a good breakfast is important."

That's bombastic. The packaging is enormous. The content is tiny.

Bombastic = language that is inflated, dramatic, and self-important, designed to impress, but ultimately empty of real meaning. It is always used as a negative label. The more bombastic something is, the bigger the gap between how impressive it sounds and how little it actually says.
1973:
Before you can truly understand this word, you need to picture what a bomb does. A bomb explodes — suddenly, violently, and without warning. It sends shockwaves outward. It changes everything around it in an instant. Nothing looks the same after a bomb goes off.

The word bombshell takes that powerful image and applies it to real-life situations. It is used to describe something — or sometimes someone — that hits with that same sudden, dramatic, overwhelming force.

Meaning 1: A Shocking Piece of News or Information

This is by far the most common way the word is used today. A bombshell is a piece of news, a statement, or a revelation that is completely unexpected and deeply shocking — the kind that stops people in their tracks and leaves them stunned.

The key qualities of a bombshell in this sense are:

  • It comes out of nowhere. Nobody saw it coming.
  • It is significant. It is not minor news — it is the kind that changes things.
  • It causes a strong emotional reaction — shock, disbelief, surprise, or even panic.

Examples:

  • "The celebrity's sudden divorce announcement was a bombshell."
  • "The scientist dropped a bombshell when he revealed that the study's results were faked."
  • "The news of the company's collapse came as a complete bombshell to its employees."

Notice the phrase "drop a bombshell" in the second example. This is extremely common. Just like a bomb is dropped, shocking news is also dropped on people — meaning it is delivered suddenly, leaving others to deal with the explosion of emotions and consequences that follow. You will hear and read this phrase very often.

More examples of "drop a bombshell":

  • "She dropped a bombshell at the dinner table by announcing she was moving abroad."
  • "The lawyer dropped a bombshell in court that changed the entire case."

A bombshell in this sense can be something heard, read, announced, or revealed. It can be a confession, a secret, a discovery, a decision, or any news that shakes the people who receive it.

Meaning 2: A Literal Bomb or Explosive Shell

In its most original, direct sense, a bombshell is an actual explosive device — specifically, a metal shell or casing filled with explosive material, designed to be fired from artillery or dropped from an aircraft, and to explode on impact.

Example:

  • "Archaeologists discovered an unexploded bombshell buried in the field from World War II."

This literal meaning is used less often in everyday conversation today, but you will encounter it in historical writing, military contexts, war journalism, and literature. It is worth knowing, but it is not the meaning most people are reaching for when they use this word in modern speech.

Meaning 3: A Strikingly Attractive Person

Informally, bombshell is also used to describe a person — most often a woman — who is considered dramatically and powerfully attractive. The idea is that their appearance hits you the way an explosion does: sudden, overwhelming, impossible to ignore.

Examples:

  • "She walked into the room looking like a total bombshell."
  • "He was considered the bombshell of the cast."

This usage is informal and colloquial — meaning it belongs to casual speech, not formal writing. You would not use it in an academic essay or a professional report. It also carries a strong physical connotation, so it is important to be aware of the social context before using it. You will encounter it frequently in entertainment journalism, casual conversation, and pop culture.

All three meanings share one unifying idea: overwhelming, sudden impact.

  • A literal bombshell explodes and destroys.
  • A news bombshell explodes into a conversation or the public consciousness and shakes everything up.
  • A bombshell person has a look that hits everyone around them like a shockwave.

Once you hold onto that central image — something that strikes hard, fast, and leaves a lasting impact — the word will always make sense to you, regardless of which meaning is being used.

Since the word has three meanings, how do you know which one is being used? Context almost always makes it clear:

  • If someone is talking about news, an announcement, or a revelation → it is Meaning 1.
  • If someone is talking about war, history, weapons, or explosives → it is Meaning 2.
  • If someone is describing a person's appearance → it is Meaning 3.
Register: When and Where Is This Word Used?

• Meaning 1 (shocking news) is used in both everyday conversation and journalism, news headlines, and media. It is very common.
  • Meaning 2 (actual bomb) is used in historical, military, and technical contexts.
  • Meaning 3 (attractive person) is informal only — casual speech and entertainment media.

Meaning 1Shocking, unexpected news or revelation that stuns people
Meaning 2An actual explosive shell or bomb
Meaning 3(Informal) A strikingly attractive person
Key phraseDrop a bombshell — to suddenly deliver shocking news
Central ideaSomething that hits suddenly with overwhelming force
1974:
A bon mot is a short, clever, and witty remark — one that is not just funny, but brilliantly phrased. It's the kind of thing someone says in conversation that makes everyone stop, smile, and think, "That was perfectly said."

It's not a long speech or a carefully prepared joke. It's a single sentence — sometimes just a few words — that lands with surprising sharpness and elegance.
The three things that make something a bon mot

A remark earns the title "bon mot" only when it has all three of these qualities:

1. Wit — It's intellectually clever. It shows a sharp, quick mind. There's a sense that the speaker saw something in the moment that others missed, and expressed it perfectly.

2. Brevity — It's short and concentrated. A bon mot is never rambling. Its power comes from compression — saying something profound or funny in as few words as possible.

3. Elegance of expression — How it's said matters just as much as what is said. The phrasing itself is part of the pleasure. A bon mot is crafted, not stumbled upon.

If a remark is clever but clumsy in expression, it's not quite a bon mot. If it's funny but shallow, it's probably just a joke. A bon mot is the perfect overlap of all three.
What a bon mot is not

Understanding what it's not will sharpen your understanding:

  • Not a joke — A joke has a setup and a punchline; it's performed. A bon mot arises naturally in conversation. It's spontaneous — or at least, it sounds that way.
  • Not a pun — A pun plays on words for a groan-worthy laugh. A bon mot aims for admiration, not groans.
  • Not an insult — Although a bon mot can sting someone, its primary quality is its wit, not its cruelty. If the cleverness disappears, what's left isn't a bon mot.
  • Not a proverb or life lesson — A proverb is timeless wisdom meant to guide. A bon mot is situational — it shines in a specific moment.

The writer and playwright Oscar Wilde was perhaps history's greatest producer of bons mots. Consider this remark of his:

"I can resist everything except temptation."

Notice how it works: in one sentence, he admits weakness while simultaneously appearing charming and self-aware. It's funny, it's paradoxical, and it's perfectly constructed. That's a bon mot.

Or this, attributed to Winston Churchill, when asked if he was drunk and disgraceful: "And you, madam, are ugly. But tomorrow I shall be sober." — Sharp, devastating, and delivered in perfect form. A bon mot.

The key is that these remarks feel inevitable — as if no other words could have said it better.

"Bon mot" is a somewhat elevated, literary word. You won't hear it in casual everyday conversation. You're more likely to encounter it in:

  • Book reviews and literary criticism
  • Discussions of famous speakers, writers, or intellectuals
  • Writing about wit, humour, or social intelligence

In a sentence:

  • "The guest lecturer was brilliant, and his bons mots kept the audience delighted throughout."
  • "She collected his bons mots the way others collect quotations."
  • "It wasn't a speech so much as a string of bons mots, each one sharper than the last."
The plural of bon mot is bons mots. When you're talking about more than one such remark, you say bons mots.
The feeling a bon mot creates

When you hear a true bon mot, it produces a specific reaction: you laugh or smile, but you also feel a little dazzled. There's a brief moment where you think, "How did they think of that so quickly?" — and even a slight envy that you didn't say it yourself.

That mixture of amusement, admiration, and slight envy is the hallmark of a successful bon mot.
A bon mot is a brilliantly witty, elegantly phrased, and perfectly timed short remark — one that makes people both laugh and marvel at how well it was said.
1975: A bon-bon is a small, sweet confection — in other words, a bite-sized candy or sweet treat. Think of it as a tiny little piece of something sweet that you can pop into your mouth in one or two bites. That's the heart of the word.

The word "bon-bon" is French in origin. In French, the word "bon" simply means "good." So "bon-bon" is literally just "good-good" — the word repeated twice. This kind of word-doubling is very common in French when talking to or about children, the way English speakers might say "night-night" instead of "night," or "choo-choo" instead of "train." It gives the word a playful, childlike, delightful quality — which makes perfect sense, because candy is something children love.

Over time, the word traveled out of France and into English, along with many other French food words (like "café," "croissant," and "soufflé"). English speakers adopted it as-is, keeping the French pronunciation and spelling.

It is pronounced: BON-bon (both syllables rhyme; the "n" is soft, almost silent in strict French pronunciation — closer to "baw(n)-baw(n)" — but in everyday English, most people say it as "BON-bon" and that is perfectly fine and widely understood).

It can be spelled either "bon-bon" (with a hyphen) or "bonbon" (no hyphen). Both spellings are correct and accepted.
What Exactly Is a Bon-Bon? (The Details)

Here is where it gets a little interesting, because the exact meaning of "bon-bon" shifts slightly depending on where you are in the world and the context you're in.

In French (the original meaning)

In French, "bonbon" is simply the everyday word for any candy or sweet. It is a general term. A child asking their parent for candy in France would say, "Je veux un bonbon" — meaning "I want a candy." So in its home language, it doesn't refer to one specific type of sweet; it covers the whole category.

In British English

In British English, "bon-bon" traditionally refers to a specific type of sweet: usually a soft, chewy candy with a sweet, flavoured centre, coated in a hard sugar shell. Think of a small, sugary-crusted candy with a yielding, slightly sticky inside. These are often fruit-flavoured (like strawberry or lemon) and come in bright colours.

In American English

In American English, "bonbon" tends to refer more specifically to a chocolate-covered candy with a soft or creamy filling inside. The filling could be fruit, fondant (a smooth, sweet paste), caramel, nuts, or cream. The outside is a thin shell of chocolate. A classic example would be a chocolate-covered cherry — soft cherry and syrup inside, chocolate shell outside. This is what most Americans picture when they hear the word.

In Fine/Artisan Chocolate-Making

In the world of high-end chocolate and professional pastry arts, "bonbon" (usually written without the hyphen in this context) has a very precise meaning: it refers to a small, moulded chocolate shell — typically made from tempered dark, milk, or white chocolate — filled with ganache, caramel, praline, fruit paste, or another flavoured filling, then sealed with a thin chocolate base.

These are the beautiful, jewel-like chocolates you see in luxury chocolate boutiques, often decorated on top with vibrant colours, edible gold, or intricate patterns. They are single-bite pieces and are considered a high art form in confectionery. Each one is carefully crafted and precisely made. This is the meaning professional chocolatiers use.
How Is a Bon-Bon Different from a Truffle?

This is a very common source of confusion, so it's worth clearing up.

  • A truffle is a specific type of bon-bon, but not all bon-bons are truffles. A truffle is traditionally a ball of ganache (a mix of chocolate and cream), sometimes rolled in cocoa powder or dipped in chocolate. Its name comes from its resemblance to the earthy truffle mushroom. Truffles tend to be rustic, round, and soft throughout.
  • A bon-bon, especially in the artisan chocolate sense, usually has a harder, precisely moulded chocolate shell on the outside with a distinct filling inside. The shell gives you a clean snap, then you experience the soft filling — whereas a truffle is soft all the way through.

So: a truffle is a type of bon-bon, but a bon-bon is a broader category that includes truffles and many other types.
What Are the Most Common Fillings?

If you're curious what can go inside a bon-bon, here are the most common ones:

Ganache — a smooth, creamy mixture of chocolate and cream. It can be flavoured with anything: vanilla, coffee, raspberry, mint, passion fruit, salted caramel, and much more. This is the most popular filling in artisan chocolates.

Caramel — thick, buttery, sweet caramel, sometimes salted (salted caramel bon-bons are hugely popular).

Praline — a paste made from ground roasted nuts (usually hazelnuts or almonds) and sugar. It has a rich, nutty flavour and a slightly grainy texture.

Fondant — a smooth, sweet sugar paste. This is the classic filling you find in older-style bon-bons, like chocolate-covered cherries with a fondant-and-syrup centre.

Fruit pastes or liqueurs — compressed fruit fillings or alcohol-based fillings (like a rum or brandy centre). Some classic bon-bons have a liquid alcoholic centre.
A Quick Summary to Lock It All In

To tie it all together: a bon-bon is a small, sweet, usually bite-sized candy. The word comes from French and literally means "good-good." Depending on where you are and the context, it might mean any candy in general (French usage), a chewy sugar-coated sweet (British usage), a chocolate-covered creamy candy (American usage), or a precisely crafted moulded chocolate with a flavoured filling (professional confectionery usage). What all these meanings share is the same soul: something small, sweet, and pleasurable.

The word has a warm, cheerful, almost child-like quality to it — which is entirely appropriate, because at the end of the day, a bon-bon is simply one of life's small, sweet joys.
1976:
"Bona fide" means genuine, real, and authentic — exactly what something or someone claims to be. When you call something bona fide, you are saying: this is the real thing, not a fake, not an imitation, not a trick.

Think of it this way: if you bought a painting that was signed "Picasso," a bona fide Picasso would mean it was truly painted by Picasso himself — not a copy, not a forgery, not a painting that merely looks like his style.

The most important idea inside "bona fide" is the absence of deception. It doesn't just mean "real" in a casual sense. It means real in a way that can be trusted and verified. There is no hidden agenda, no fraud, no pretending involved.

This is why the word is often used when someone's legitimacy is being questioned or confirmed. You reach for "bona fide" precisely when you want to settle a doubt — to say: yes, this person or thing is exactly what it appears to be.

This is crucial: "bona fide" is about authenticity, not quality. It does not mean something is good, impressive, or excellent. It only means it is genuine.

  • A bona fide mistake is a real mistake — not an impressive one.
  • A bona fide failure is a true failure — not a noble one.

So if someone says "that was a bona fide disaster," they mean it was a genuine, undeniable disaster — not that the disaster was somehow admirable.
How It Feels in a Sentence

"Bona fide" carries a slightly emphatic, confirmatory energy. Saying "she's a bona fide expert" feels stronger than simply saying "she's a real expert." It has a sense of I am vouching for this — there is no question about it. It pushes back against doubt with confidence.

People:

  • "He is a bona fide scientist" — He genuinely is a scientist. He has the credentials, the training, and the expertise. He isn't just playing one or claiming to be one.
  • "She became a bona fide celebrity overnight" — She is a real, undeniable celebrity now — not a minor or questionable one.

Things and situations:

  • "This is a bona fide emergency" — This is a real emergency, not an exaggeration or a false alarm.
  • "They made a bona fide offer to buy the house" — The offer was sincere and serious, not a casual or dishonest one.
  • "That record is a bona fide classic" — It is genuinely, indisputably a classic — confirmed by time and recognition.

In legal and formal settings:
"Bona fide" is used a lot in law. A bona fide purchaser is someone who bought something honestly — they paid a fair price and had no idea the item was stolen or had any hidden legal problems. Here, the word emphasizes that the person acted with honesty and good faith, without any intent to deceive.
The Difference Between Bona Fide and Similar Words

• Real is simple and neutral. "A real doctor."
  • Genuine emphasizes that something is not a copy or imitation. "A genuine signature."
  • Legitimate emphasizes that something follows the proper rules or standards. "A legitimate business."
  • Bona fide combines elements of all three — it says something is real, not imitated, and can be trusted as exactly what it claims to be. It also carries a slightly more formal, confirmatory weight than the others.

Anything described as bona fide stands in direct contrast to things that are: fake, fraudulent, counterfeit, pretend, phony, or a sham. If a bona fide diamond is the real gemstone, a non-bona fide one is a piece of glass dressed up to look like it.

"Bona fide" naturally appears before nouns like: expert, offer, member, resident, emergency, classic, star, talent, deal, reason, and mistake. You will almost always see it placed directly before the noun it describes.
"Bona fide" means something or someone is completely genuine — truly what it claims to be — with no deception, no fraud, and no imitation involved.
1977:
A bonanza is a sudden, large source of great wealth, profit, or something extremely valuable and desirable. Think of it as a moment or a situation where good things — usually money or resources — flow in much, much more than expected or than usual.

The single most important thing to understand is this: a bonanza is not just "a good thing." It is an overwhelmingly good thing. The scale and abundance are what define it.

Imagine you own a small farm. One year, due to perfect weather, your harvest is ten times bigger than normal. You sell everything and make more money than you've ever made in your life. That harvest is a bonanza.

Now imagine a company releases a product, and it unexpectedly sells millions of copies overnight. That moment is a bonanza for the company.

The word captures that feeling of striking it enormously rich — of abundance arriving in a big, often surprising way.
The Three Key Qualities of a Bonanza

For something to qualify as a bonanza, it typically has these qualities:

1. Great scale or abundance
A bonanza is never small. It involves a large, impressive amount — of money, profit, opportunity, or resources. If something is just "a little extra," it is not a bonanza.

2. A strong sense of good fortune
A bonanza is always a positive thing. It benefits someone. There is no such thing as a "bad bonanza." The word has an inherently cheerful, exciting energy to it.

3. A feeling of windfall or unexpected richness
A bonanza often (though not always) carries a sense of something that came in more generously than expected. It feels like luck, even when it results from hard work — because the scale of reward feels extraordinary.
What a Bonanza Can Refer To

The word is flexible. A bonanza can be:

  • A situation — "The oil discovery was a bonanza for the country."
  • A time period — "Last year was a bonanza year for the film industry."
  • A source of profit or gain — "The new law turned out to be a bonanza for large corporations."
  • An event or occurrence — "The holiday shopping season is a bonanza for retailers."
  • A literal physical discovery (in its original mining sense) — "The miners hit a bonanza deep in the mountain."

Notice how the word can be applied in finance, business, farming, politics, entertainment, and everyday life. Its use is wide.

Bonanza is not a dry or neutral word. It carries enthusiasm and excitement. When you use it, you are not just reporting a fact — you are conveying a sense of wow, that's a lot, that's incredible. Journalists and writers often use it to make headlines more vivid and energetic.

It sits in a slightly informal register, which means it is very common in newspapers, magazines, and everyday speech, but you might avoid it in the most formal academic writing.
Collocations — Words That Naturally Go With "Bonanza"

Here are the most natural and common ways the word appears:

  • a bonanza for [someone] — "The deal was a bonanza for investors."
  • a bonanza of [something] — "A bonanza of opportunities opened up."
  • a bonanza year/season/period — "Farmers are hoping for a bonanza season."
  • strike a bonanza — "The company struck a bonanza with its new product."
  • reap a bonanza — "Early investors reaped a bonanza when the stock soared."
  • an economic/financial bonanza — "Tourism became an economic bonanza for the small town."
  • a windfall bonanza — used when the good fortune is especially sudden and unexpected.
How It Differs From Similar Words

• Windfall — Also means unexpected good fortune, but a windfall is usually a one-time event (like receiving an inheritance). A bonanza can describe an ongoing rich situation, not just a single moment.
  • Jackpot — More specifically tied to gambling and luck; more casual and playful. A bonanza sounds more substantial and weighty.
  • Godsend — Focuses on how desperately welcome something is. A bonanza focuses on the scale of what arrived, not necessarily the need for it.
  • Boom — A boom describes a general period of rapid growth (an economic boom). A bonanza is more specific — it describes a particularly rich, rewarding outcome for someone or something.

• It does not mean just "a good deal" or "a bargain." The scale matters.
  • It does not carry any sense of hardship or negativity. You will never see it used to describe something bad happening to someone.
  • It is not the same as simply "a lot of something." A traffic jam is a lot of cars, but it is not a bonanza. The abundance in a bonanza is always desirable.

A bonanza (noun) is a situation, source, event, or period that brings an exceptionally large amount of wealth, profit, or something greatly valued — often in a way that feels extraordinarily fortunate. It always implies abundance, positivity, and impressive scale.

If you ever see the word and feel unsure, ask yourself: Is someone or something receiving a large, exciting, rewarding flow of something good? If yes — that is a bonanza.
1978: A bond is something that connects, holds, or ties things together — whether those things are people, objects, atoms, or agreements. Think of it as an invisible or visible "link" between two or more things. Every meaning of this word comes back to that central idea of connection and holding.

This is the most everyday meaning. When two people (or a person and an animal) feel a strong sense of closeness, loyalty, or love for each other, that feeling is called a bond.

Examples:

  • The bond between a mother and her child is one of the strongest known to humans.
  • After years of working together through tough times, the soldiers formed an unbreakable bond.
  • A dog often develops a deep bond with its owner.

Think of it as an invisible thread connecting two hearts. You can't see it or touch it, but you can feel it — and it's real. The stronger the shared experiences, trust, and love, the stronger the bond.

A bond can also mean a serious, binding promise — one that you are morally or legally expected to keep. When someone says "my word is my bond," they mean their promise is as solid and trustworthy as a written contract.

Examples:

  • The two business partners shook hands, and for them, that handshake was a bond.
  • He gave his bond that he would return the money within a year.

Here, the "connection" is between a person and their word — they are tied to what they have promised.

In the world of finance and investing, a bond is a type of loan — but one that works in reverse from how most people think of loans.

Here's how it works simply:

  • A government or company needs to borrow a large amount of money.
  • Instead of going to one bank, they borrow from thousands of ordinary people (investors).
  • Each investor buys a "bond" for a fixed price (say, $1,000).
  • The government or company promises to pay the investor regular interest (called a coupon) over a set number of years.
  • At the end of that period (the maturity date), they return the original $1,000 to the investor.

So a bond is essentially a formal IOU with a fixed schedule of repayment and interest.

Examples:

  • The US government issues Treasury bonds to fund public spending.
  • She invested her savings in corporate bonds to earn steady interest income.
  • The city issued bonds to raise money for building a new hospital.

Why is it called a "bond"? Because it binds the borrower legally to pay back the money as promised.

Key terms you'll hear with financial bonds:

  • Issuer — the one who creates and sells the bond (the borrower: a government, city, or company).
  • Bondholder — the person who buys the bond (the lender/investor).
  • Coupon rate — the interest rate paid to the bondholder.
  • Maturity — the date when the loan ends and the original money is paid back.
  • Face value / Par value — the original amount the bond is worth (e.g., $1,000).

In chemistry, a bond is the force that holds atoms together to form molecules. Atoms are the tiny building blocks of everything, and a chemical bond is what "glues" them to each other.

Examples:

  • Water (H₂O) exists because two hydrogen atoms are bonded to one oxygen atom.
  • The bond between atoms in a diamond is so strong that it makes diamond one of the hardest substances on Earth.

There are different types of chemical bonds (covalent, ionic, hydrogen, metallic), each describing how atoms share or transfer electrons to stick together — but the idea is always the same: a bond is the connection that holds atoms in place relative to each other.
5. Physical Bonds — Chains, Ropes, or Restraints

In an older and more literal sense, bonds (often used in the plural) refers to physical things that restrain or imprison someone — like chains, ropes, handcuffs, or shackles.

Examples:

  • The prisoner struggled to break free from his bonds.
  • She was held in bonds and couldn't escape.

This meaning is less common in everyday modern speech, but you'll encounter it frequently in literature, historical texts, and religious writings (e.g., "breaking the bonds of slavery").
6. An Adhesive Bond (in materials and construction)

When two surfaces stick together — because of glue, cement, heat, or another substance — the connection formed between them is called a bond.

Examples:

  • The glue created a strong bond between the two pieces of wood.
  • The weld formed a permanent bond between the metal parts.
  • A good primer improves the bond between paint and the wall.

Here, the word describes how well and how tightly two surfaces cling to each other.
7. A Surety Bond or Bail Bond (Legal)

In legal and insurance contexts, a bond is a formal financial guarantee that someone will fulfill an obligation — and if they don't, the person or company who issued the bond will pay the penalty.

  • A bail bond: When someone is arrested and the court sets a bail amount (say, $10,000), a bail bond is a guarantee (often provided by a bail bondsman) that the accused will show up for their court date. If the accused runs away, the bondsman pays the court.
  • A surety bond: A contractor might be required to hold a surety bond before starting a construction project. If they fail to complete the work as promised, the bond pays the client for the loss.

Think of it as a financial safety net backed by a promise.
8. A Bond in Bricklaying and Construction

In construction, a bond refers to the pattern or arrangement in which bricks, stones, or blocks are laid so that the joints between them are staggered. This staggering makes a wall much stronger.

Examples:

  • The mason used a running bond to build the garden wall (where each brick overlaps the one below it by half).
  • Different types of bonds — like the Flemish bond or English bond — create different patterns and strengths.

Even though "bond" has many different meanings across different fields, they all share the same soul: a connection that holds things together and carries a sense of obligation, strength, or commitment. Whether it's the love between two people, an atom holding to another, a legal contract, or a brick interlocked with its neighbor — a bond is what keeps things from falling apart.

Here's a quick mental map of all the meanings:

  • People → emotional closeness and loyalty
  • Promises → a commitment you are bound to keep
  • Finance → a formal loan with fixed repayment terms
  • Chemistry → the force holding atoms together
  • Restraints → chains or ropes that physically bind someone
  • Surfaces → the sticking together of materials
  • Legal/Insurance → a financial guarantee of performance
  • Construction → the pattern of laying bricks for strength
1979: To bond means to join or connect things — or people — so closely that they become firmly tied to each other. That connection can be physical (like glue holding two surfaces together), chemical (like atoms joining to form a substance), emotional (like two friends growing deeply close), or even legal and financial. The word always carries the same essential idea: two or more things come together and stay together.
Sense 1: To Form an Emotional Connection

This is the most common everyday use of the word. When people bond, they develop a warm, genuine, close relationship with one another — a connection that feels strong and lasting.

Examples:

  • She bonded with her college roommate on the very first night.
  • The team bonded during the difficult project they worked on together.
  • New parents often bond deeply with their baby in the first few weeks.

Notice two important patterns here:

"Bond with" someone — this tells you who you are connecting with.
He bonded with his grandfather over summers spent fishing.

"Bond over" something — this tells you what brought you together, the shared thing that created the connection.
The two strangers bonded over their love of old movies.

Bonding between people isn't forced or instant. It builds naturally through shared experiences, trust, vulnerability, or time spent together. You cannot make yourself bond with someone — it happens. This is why we say people "bond" rather than simply "become friends." Bonding suggests a deeper, more instinctive kind of closeness — the kind a mother feels with her child, or soldiers feel after going through hardship together.
Sense 2: To Stick or Join Physically

When a material, substance, or surface bonds, it sticks firmly and tightly to another surface — usually through an adhesive (like glue), heat, pressure, or a chemical reaction. The result is that the two things are held together and are difficult or impossible to separate.

Examples:

  • This industrial glue bonds metal to glass in under a minute.
  • The tiles have bonded permanently to the concrete floor.
  • The layers of the material bond when exposed to heat.

You'll notice "bond" can be used in two ways here:

Transitive (the glue does the bonding to something): The adhesive bonds the pieces together.

Intransitive (the materials bond on their own): The surfaces have bonded.

Both are correct and common.

In chemistry, atoms and molecules bond when they link together to form a new, larger structure. This happens when atoms share or exchange electrons. The result is a chemical compound — a completely new substance.

Examples:

  • Carbon atoms bond with hydrogen atoms to form hydrocarbons.
  • Oxygen and hydrogen bond to create water.
  • The atoms bond together through a process called covalent bonding.

This is a technical use, but it's the same idea — two things come together and stay together firmly.
Sense 4: To Guarantee or Secure (Legal/Financial Use)

This use is more formal and specialized, but worth knowing. In legal and financial contexts, to bond someone or something means to secure them through a guarantee — a kind of formal promise backed by money — that ensures they will fulfill their obligations honestly.

In practice, you'll most often see this in the past participle form: bonded.

Examples:

  • All our workers are fully bonded and insured. (meaning: their employer has taken out a financial guarantee covering any dishonest or harmful acts they might commit)
  • The contractor must be bonded before starting the job. (meaning: they must have a surety bond — a financial safety net for the client)

If a business says their staff are "bonded," they mean that if an employee steals from you or causes damage, there is a financial policy in place to cover your loss. It is a mark of trustworthiness and professional accountability.

Even across these very different uses, one thread runs through all of them: a bond is not a loose or casual connection. Whether it's glue holding two tiles together, atoms forming a molecule, two people growing close through shared experience, or a legal guarantee tying a contractor to their obligations — bonding always implies a connection that is strong, lasting, and not easily broken. The verb captures that quality of things being genuinely, firmly held together.
Common Collocations (Words That Often Appear with "Bond")

• bond with — connect emotionally with someone
  • bond over — connect because of a shared interest or experience
  • bond together — join as a unified group or mass
  • quickly bond / instantly bond — form a connection rapidly
  • bond to a surface — adhere physically
  • fully bonded — legally/financially guaranteed

When used emotionally, "bond" carries a sense of warmth and depth. To say two people "bonded" is to say something meaningful happened between them — not just that they got along, but that something genuine and lasting was built. This is why "bond" is often used when describing relationships under pressure or difficulty: soldiers, teammates, survivors, new parents. Those are the conditions where real bonds form.
